## Page 1


Nyquist Signaling Modulation (NSM): An FTN-Inspired
Paradigm Shift in Modulation Design for 6G and Beyond
Mohamed Siala1
Abdullah Al-Nafisah2
Tareq Al-Naffouri2
1Higher School of Communications of Tunis (SUP’COM), Carthage University, Tunis, Tunisia
2Computer, Electrical and Mathematical Sciences and Engineering (CEMSE), King Abdullah
University of Science and Technology (KAUST), Thuwal, Saudi Arabia
mohamed.siala@supcom.tn
{abdullah.alnafisah, tareq.alnaffouri}@kaust.edu.sa
November 12, 2025
arXiv:2511.08553v1  [eess.SP]  11 Nov 2025


## Page 2


Abstract
Nyquist Signaling Modulations (NSMs) are a novel signaling paradigm inspired by faster-
than-Nyquist principles but following a fundamentally different approach that enables controlled
inter-symbol interference through carefully designed finite-impulse-response filters. NSMs can be
realized in one-, two-, and three-dimensional configurations using rational- or real-tapped filters,
providing increased degrees of freedom for filter design, energy balancing, and preservation of
minimum squared Euclidean distances (MSED). This structured approach offers a flexible and
analytically tractable framework that can enhance robustness, spectral efficiency, and performance
relative to classical modulation schemes.
NSMs are systematically optimized through rational- or real-valued finite-impulse-response
filters. Rational-tap filters allow direct derivation of closed-form filter expressions and support
tractable exhaustive searches using equivalence-class reductions, even for relatively long filter lengths.
Real-tap filters, in contrast, provide a larger space of candidate NSMs, which can improve achievable
performance, although their optimization is more intricate and rapidly becomes intractable as
filter length increases. For these filters, closed-form expressions for the filter structures can be
derived indirectly via symbolic calculus, but only for relatively short filter lengths within the
tractable optimization range. Multidimensional extensions of NSMs further increase design flexibility,
enabling the preservation of the 2-ASK minimum squared Euclidean distance across substreams.
The performance of NSMs is analyzed using a transfer-function framework, including full, reduced,
and truncated representations as well as iterative computational methods, which accurately capture
dominant error events and yield BEP bounds in very tight agreement with simulated BER across
extended SNR ranges. These transfer functions are structurally similar to those of convolutional
codes but exhibit radically distinct error behaviors due to the exponential decay of error-event
significance with the Hamming weight of their input differences.
Beyond one-dimensional structures, NSMs generalize and extend the multistream FTN (MFTN)
concept to two-, three-, and mixed-dimensional configurations, offering additional degrees of freedom
for arranging substreams and controlling inter-substream interference while preserving minimum
squared Euclidean distances. Detection complexity naturally increases with dimensionality. To
address this, we propose a two-stage maximum-likelihood detector that substantially reduces
computational effort. Nevertheless, its complexity remains non-negligible, motivating further research
into reduced-complexity and iterative detection schemes such as sphere decoding.
A unified analytical framework supports the optimization and evaluation of NSMs, particularly for
rational-tapped filters, where equivalence relations and MSED-preserving transformations drastically
reduce the search space and enable systematic exploration of high-dimensional configurations.
Reduced and truncated transfer-function methodologies, validated through extensive simulations,
provide tight analytical bounds on bit-error probability and confirm the predictive accuracy of the
theoretical models across wide SNR ranges.
NSMs are further generalized within an analog Low-Density Generator Matrix (LDGM) frame-
work, which relaxes the rigid structure of conventional NSMs and introduces controlled sparsity
and randomness across generating matrices. This added flexibility enables better control of energy
distribution and structural regularity, helping to mitigate low-distance error events and enhance
robustness. The analog LDGM formulation also provides a coherent foundation for the seamless
and harmonious integration of channel coding, or jointly channel and source coding, with the
modulation process, forming a unified and highly adaptable signal representation paradigm. Within
this framework, energy balancing, interleaving, and message-passing strategies play a central role in
mitigating low-distance and low-Hamming-weight error events, thereby reinforcing the structural
and performance robustness of NSMs in both coded and uncoded scenarios.
Collectively, these developments establish a coherent foundation for the next generation of
physical-layer architectures. By naturally combining modulation with source and/or channel coding
within a single, continuous design space, the NSM–analog LDGM paradigm introduces a flexible,


## Page 3


scalable, and performance-driven alternative to classical modulations. Its structural compatibility
with modern LDPC-based coding schemes and its ability to harmonize controlled interference,
sparsity, and joint optimization make it a strong candidate for future 6G and beyond communication
standards.
Keywords: Nyquist Signaling Modulations (NSMs), Faster-than-Nyquist (FTN), Multistream
Faster-than-Nyquist (MFTN), Minimum Squared Euclidean Distance (MSED), Analog LDGM NSMs,
Multidimensional NSMs, Multi-Stream Partial-Response Signaling (MS-PRS), Energy balancing, Tight-
ness, Reduced transfer function, Truncated transfer function, Closed-form filter derivation, Digital–analog
packing, Joint source-channel-modulation design, 6G communications, Next-generation wireless systems,
Future physical-layer design

1 to S −1. The node combines all intrinsic messages from parity-check nodes except
the one it is replying to, together with intrinsic information from the analog domain,
enforcing consistency and producing an enhanced extrinsic message sent back to the
sidelined parity-check node. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

Equality constraint enforcement at the binary variable node during the final (S-th)
digital sub-iteration. All intrinsic messages from parity-check nodes are combined without
exclusion to produce a final enhanced extrinsic message. This message is then passed
transparently through the binary-to-bipolar conversion interface back to the bipolar
variable node in the analog domain. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

Y-shaped factor graph representing the joint integration of source coding, modulation,
and LDPC parity constraints through the shared binary vector ¯b. The left branch models
lossy source quantization via the synthesis matrix GF, the right branch handles analog
LDGM NSM through GM, and the lower branch enforces LDPC code membership using
the parity-check matrix H.

77
Stratified instantaneous power profiles in the full-dimensional-span case for q = 40,
n = 60, and k = 120. Each colored layer represents the squared values of a single bipolar
symbol’s row in the reconstruction matrix GF (panel a) or the generating matrix GM
(panel b). Here, each row spans the full output dimension, resulting in globally distributed
and relatively uniform profiles. Rows are normalized to unit energy for visualization and
stacked vertically to reveal the structured energy distribution across dimensions. The
vertical scaling between panels reflects the n/q = 60/40 = 3/2 ratio between modulation
and source dimensions.
. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
258
78
Stratified instantaneous power profiles in the limited-dimensional-span case for parameters
q = 40, n = 60, and k = 120. Each row in GF and GM contributes energy over a restricted
support: 10 dimensions in the source domain and 15 dimensions in the modulation domain,
respectively, simulating localized interactions. This localization leads to sharper and
more concentrated energy patterns, particularly in the source domain. As in the full-span
case, each row is normalized to unit energy for visualization, and the panels maintain
the 3/2 vertical scaling between modulation and source dimensions.

Introduction
The exponential growth of wireless connectivity and high-speed multimedia services has placed un-
precedented pressure on spectral resources. Bandwidth efficiency, defined as the average data rate
per unit bandwidth, has therefore become a central design metric for next-generation mobile systems.
Conventional transmission architectures follow the Nyquist criterion. This ensures time-orthogonality
and eliminates Inter-Symbol interference (ISI) at a symbol spacing tied to the signal bandwidth.
FTN signaling departs from this orthogonality constraint by intentionally increasing the symbol
packing density in time. The technique accepts controlled ISI in exchange for higher spectral efficiency.
Mazo [1] demonstrated that, for ideal “sinc” pulses in continuous time, the symbol rate may be
increased by up to 25% without reducing the Minimum Squared Euclidean Distance (MSED) between
distinct transmitted sequences. This establishes an information-theoretic and geometrical basis for
FTN’s potential to improve throughput without immediate penalty to error performance at high
Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR).
While Mazo’s original treatment was cast in continuous time, practical realizations require discrete-
time models and finite-length processing. McGuire and Sima [2] introduced a block-based discrete-time
reformulation of FTN. In their approach, rectangular frequency-domain shaping over finite blocks
yields aliased, “sinc”-like discrete pulses and limits the ISI span to a finite number of samples. This
block formulation bounds receiver complexity and enables parallelizable detection algorithms. It makes
FTN detection tractable for real systems while retaining the distance-preserving intuition of the
continuous-time theory.
A conceptually related but differently motivated line of work is represented by the Signal Codes of
Shalvi [3]. In their original interpretation, Signal Codes modify the signal geometry in Euclidean space
with the goal of maximizing the MSED between constellation points for a given data rate. The approach
emphasizes coding gain rather than bandwidth gain. A complementary interpretation, which is of
particular relevance here, is to view the same mechanism as a means of preserving the MSED when the
data rate is increased. In this dual perspective, Signal Codes conceptually achieve the same overarching
goal as FTN: enabling data rate growth without sacrificing distance properties. Although practical
implementations of Signal Codes are hindered by the need for additional shaping and power-control
procedures to ensure spectral efficiency, their structural resemblance to filter-based FTN frameworks
makes them an instructive analogue for the schemes proposed in this work.
FTN signaling has also been extended to Multi-Carrier (MC) systems, giving rise to Multi-Carrier
FTN (MFTN), also referred to as time-frequency packing. The first study of MFTN was reported by
Rusek and Anderson [4]. In MFTN, non-orthogonal symbol packing occurs along two axes, creating
a multi-dimensional signaling structure. This generalization allows higher spectral efficiency while
retaining manageable interference through advanced receiver processing. MFTN serves as an inspiration
for considering multi-dimensional modulation frameworks. In the proposed framework, these additional
dimensions are abstract and not tied to time or frequency interpretations, and the structure can, in
principle, be generalized beyond two dimensions.
Beyond MC systems, FTN principles have also been applied to Multiple-Input Multiple-Output
(MIMO) and higher-order modulation frameworks [5]. In addition, FTN shares a strong conceptual
analogy with Partial Response Signaling (PRS), and several studies treat PRS and FTN in a unified
framework or employ PRS-inspired equalization techniques within FTN systems [6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11].
These extensions illustrate the flexibility of FTN in enhancing spectral and energy efficiency and
highlight the wide applicability of bandwidth-efficient signaling techniques.
1


## Page 28


Over the past two decades, research on FTN has evolved from foundational theoretical studies to
extensive investigations into receiver architectures, coding strategies, and advanced system designs.
The sustained academic and industrial attention it has received underscores FTN’s relevance as both a
conceptual and practical paradigm for achieving higher spectral efficiency.
Figure 1 provides an overview of the evolution of FTN-related research activity between 2001 and
2023, illustrating the estimated number of publications per year. The trend clearly indicates a notable
resurgence of interest during the 2014–2018 period, coinciding with the introduction of low-complexity
detection algorithms, iterative receivers, and practical precoding techniques that made FTN increasingly
feasible for implementation. Following this peak, the figure shows continued and stable publication
activity through 2023, suggesting that FTN has matured into a stable and active area of research rather
than a transient topic of interest. This sustained output reflects the community’s ongoing efforts to
extend FTN principles to broader system paradigms, including multi-dimensional modulation, coded
systems, and machine-learning-assisted detection.
Figure 1: Estimated number of FTN-related publications per year (2001–2023), showing journal and
conference contributions. The statistics confirm the resurgence of interest around 2014–2018 and stable,
continuing activity through 2023.
Collectively, these studies outline the principal algorithmic tools underpinning modern FTN im-
plementations, including trellis-based detection, sphere decoding, frequency-domain equalization, and
precoding [6, 7, 8, 12, 10, 13]. The continuous exploration of these tools reinforces FTN’s position as a
cornerstone in the pursuit of spectrally efficient signaling for next-generation communication systems.
The present work adopts a strictly discrete-time perspective inspired by the continuous-time FTN
intuition of Mazo [1] and the discrete block formulation of McGuire and Sima [2]. Mazo’s original
contribution established that introducing intentional ISI through FTN signaling can enable higher
data rates without degrading performance. McGuire later demonstrated that this principle can be
reformulated in a discrete-time framework, showing that FTN signaling can be implemented in practice
using block-based methods. In parallel, the work of Shalvi on Signal Codes [3] provides a structural
analogue in which filter-based signal transformations preserve distance properties and inspire our
modulation and shaping strategies. Together, these three perspectives form the conceptual foundation
2


## Page 29


of our approach and naturally lead to the problem formulation, research objectives, and methodological
contributions that are developed in the remainder of this introduction.
Building on the seminal work of Mazo [1] on FTN signaling, we propose a new paradigm and
architecture for our main modulation scheme, which we refer to as NSM. While Mazo used continuous-
time “sinc” waveforms with an oversampling of the modulated signal at the same rate as the data
symbols, our approach reinterprets the continuous-time modulated signal as a discrete-time signal
sampled at exactly the Nyquist rate, in accordance with the Shannon sampling theorem. This ensures
that no information about the transmitted symbols is lost.
In our framework, the Mazo-modulated signal can be viewed as a multi-stream polyphase structure,
where each stream is filtered with an appropriately phased version of the original “sinc” waveform. This
interpretation naturally leads to a general family of NSM schemes, referred to as MS-PRS modulations.
In these modulations, the data stream from the encoder is first de-multiplexed into k parallel sub-streams.
Each sub-stream is then over-sampled by a factor of n, inserting n −1 zeros between successive samples,
and filtered by an independently designed digital filter. The outputs of all filtered sub-streams are
summed to form the composite modulated signal. Consequently, the overall modulation rate is scaled
by a factor of ρm = k/n, while the total system rate becomes ρ = ρcρm when combined with an
error-correction code of rate ρc. This architecture, illustrated in Figure 2, highlights the structural
simplicity and flexibility of the proposed MS-PRS modulation.
Figure 2: Proposed MS-PRS structure with rate ρm = k/n. Each data stream is over-sampled, filtered,
and combined to produce the modulated signal.
A distinctive property of the MS-PRS framework is that the filters applied to each sub-stream can
be chosen freely and independently from any underlying continuous-time waveform. These filters can
be of Finite Impulse Response (FIR) type, allowing simplified signal generation at the transmitter,
reduced detection complexity at the receiver, and elimination of truncation effects inherent to classical
FTN implementations, where oversampled “sinc” filters typically have Infinite Impulse Responses (IIRs).
This decoupling of the digital sub-stream filters from the analog shaping filter provides a high degree of
design flexibility and enables direct optimization of pulse characteristics according to desired system
objectives, such as maximizing the MSED or minimizing the Symbol Error Probability (SEP), with or
without channel coding.
3


## Page 30


From a broader perspective, the NSM family provides a unified framework encompassing these
multi-stream modulations. The proposed MS-PRS scheme represents its fundamental one-dimensional
realization, conceptually aligned with the classical Single-Carrier (SC) framework: a single encoded
data sequence is distributed across multiple parallel filtered paths that jointly form the transmitted
modulated signal. This structure can be interpreted as a form of analog-domain error correction that
complements digital coding, offering a more flexible and efficient alternative to conventional FTN
signaling while retaining compatibility with existing transceiver architectures.
Inspired by MFTN [7], we extend the NSM framework to Two-Dimensional (2D) and Three-
Dimensional (3D) systems. In the 2D case, the main data stream is demultiplexed into multiple
sub-streams organized on a 2D grid, filtered with freely chosen 2D FIR filters, and transmitted via
single- or multi-carrier systems, optionally using MIMO systems. Similarly, 3D NSMs demultiplex data
streams along a 3D grid and apply freely chosen 3D FIR filters. These multi-dimensional NSMs provide
additional design degrees of freedom and facilitate achieving the MSED of 2-ASK more easily than the
One-Dimensional (1D), SC case.
We consider specific families of NSMs based on their transmission rates. We study rate-2 NSMs,
which have been the main focus of historical FTN research [6], corresponding in terms of spectral
efficiency to 1D 4-ASK or 2D 16-QAM modulations. We also study rate-3 NSMs, equivalent to 1D
8-ASK or 2D 64-QAM modulations in spectral efficiency. Additionally, we consider NSMs with rates
below 2, expressed as (Q + 1)/Q for an integer Q ≥2. These lower-rate NSMs provide a tradeoff
between transmission rate and performance, and are inspired by the original Mazo FTN work, which
focused on rates around 5/4 (the Mazo’s maximum compression factor of 0.802, which preserves the
MSED of 2-ASK, yields an effective rate close to 5/4).
Within the 1D NSM framework, we propose two families of MS-PRS modulations using FIR filters.
The first family employs filters with real-valued taps, while the second uses rational or integer-valued
taps after renormalization. Filter lengths are fixed to maintain manageable processing complexity at
both transmitter and receiver. For rate-2 NSMs with real-valued filters, two categories are considered:
unconstrained, where the sub-stream filters can share the overall average modulated symbol energy
freely, and constrained, where this average energy is distributed equally among the sub-stream filters.
Unconstrained NSMs achieve higher MSEDs and provide a better bootstrap for iterative turbo-
equalization at low SNR, whereas constrained NSMs offer balanced energy distribution that benefits
performance at later iterations.
For 1D rate-2 NSMs with real-valued taps, the optimization of filters begins with a random search
procedure that approximates the identification of filter sets maximizing the MSED, up to the limits of
numerical precision. This initial step is refined through a three-stage methodology. First, promising
candidate filters are retained in numerical form. Second, the error events corresponding to the MSED
are determined exactly. Finally, exploiting the fact that these error events all yield the same MSED, we
derive a system of equations whose symbolic solution provides closed-form expressions for both the
optimal filters and the associated MSEDs, yielding exact analytical characterizations for many of the
considered configurations.
A notable structural observation concerns rate-2 NSMs where one filter has length 1 and the other
has variable length. In this case, achieving an MSED equal to that of 2-ASK requires the longer filter to
have length at least 10. For shorter lengths, the attainable distance is strictly smaller. In this context, we
also introduce the notion of tightness, which designates configurations in which the minimum distance is
attained with high multiplicity of error events. While the implications of this property will be addressed
4


## Page 31


later, the definition itself provides an additional criterion for analyzing and classifying NSMs beyond
minimum distance alone.
For rate-3 NSMs with real-valued taps, no attempt is made to derive closed-form symbolic charac-
terizations. Two complementary optimization approaches are considered. In the first, filter optimization
is carried out entirely through numerical search procedures, yielding approximate identification of filters
that maximize the MSED. In the second, rate-3 NSMs are constructed by inheriting optimized rate-2
filters and appending a third sub-stream filtered by a properly scaled impulse response of length one.
Depending on the configuration, these two approaches either converge to the same filters or yield distinct
solutions. The reasons underlying these similarities and differences are analyzed in detail, providing
additional insight into the structure of rate-3 NSMs.
A second family of NSMs is based on rational-tap filters (or equivalently, integer taps after renor-
malization). In the 1D rate-2 case, we first focus on the special scenario where the non-null taps are
bipolar. This allows a rigorous algebraic characterization of performance, employing tools such as
m-sequences and their correlation properties to analyze precisely how the structure of these integer-tap
filters determines the MSED. This algebraic study provides exact insights into the performance of
this constrained class of NSMs. Subsequently, we consider the more general 1D rate-2 NSMs with
arbitrary rational-tap filters. While these more general filters are not analyzed algebraically, they are
studied thoroughly through numerical design and optimization. The additional freedom in selecting tap
values enables improved NSM performance by expanding the design space beyond the constraints of
the bipolar-tap case.
Multi-dimensional rate-2 NSMs, as well as 1D rate-(Q + 1)/Q NSMs with Q ≥2, make use of
rational-tap filters (equivalently, integer-tap filters after renormalization) to simplify the optimization
process and keep the search space tractable. In the 2D and 3D cases, full characterization of the MSED
is not feasible due to the absence of a trellis structure. Therefore, a partial optimization is performed by
extracting 1D NSMs along key axes—such as horizontal, vertical, and diagonal axes in two dimensions,
or horizontal, vertical, depth, and Edge-to-Edge (E2E) axes in three dimensions—and maximizing
the minimum of the MSEDs of these extracted 1D systems. While this approach provides a tractable
design methodology, it does not guarantee that the overall multi-dimensional NSM will achieve the
same MSED, since error events that are not captured by the extracted 1D NSMs may exist and could
lead to lower Squared Euclidean Distances (SEDs) in the full 2D or 3D system.
Our framework enables the use of very short filters for each sub-stream, avoiding the truncation
issues encountered in classical FTN and MFTN. This significantly simplifies detection while maintaining
performance. One-dimensional NSMs naturally correspond to SC systems. In contrast, 2D and 3D
NSMs demultiplex the data streams along 2D or 3D grids, respectively, and apply freely chosen 2D or
3D FIR filters. These multi-dimensional NSMs can be transmitted over single- or multi-carrier channels,
optionally using MIMO. With two- and three-dimensional NSMs, the MSED of 2-ASK is achieved more
easily and naturally, allowing most of the time intuitive selection of the appropriate multi-dimensional
filters.
To evaluate the performance of the proposed NSMs, simulation results are obtained in terms of raw
Bit Error Rate (BER). To complement these simulations and provide analytical insight, BEP bounds
are derived from state diagrams that characterize all possible error events (including both dominant
and non-dominant ones). These diagrams provide a comprehensive view of the NSM error structure
and form the foundation for subsequent Transfer Function (TF) analyses.
In order to analyze the error events of NSMs, we build on the classical framework of convolutional
codes, where TFs are widely used to enumerate and characterize error sequences. Similarly, the TF of
5


## Page 32


an NSM depends on two symbolic parameters: N, which accounts for differences in input sequences,
and D, which characterizes the corresponding differences in output sequences. By depending on these
two parameters, the TF provides a complete representation of all possible error events. A simplified tool,
the RTF, is introduced to ease evaluation. It depends only on the parameter D, preserving the meaning
of D from the full TF while discarding the explicit tracking of input differences. This simplification
makes the RTF far more tractable for both symbolic and numerical analysis.
Truncated versions of either the TF or the RTF are considered only when direct, one-shot symbolic
computation of the full function is either impossible or prohibitively time-consuming. These truncated
versions allow focusing on the most relevant error events, particularly those associated with the lowest
SEDs, without losing the ability to characterize the dominant contributors to NSM performance. For
non-truncated TFs or RTFs, exact symbolic determination is performed directly whenever feasible. When
working with truncated versions, a finite iterative procedure is applied to compute them. Convergence of
the truncated RTF is guaranteed after a finite number of iterations in all cases. In contrast, convergence
of the truncated full TF is ensured only for non-degenerate NSMs, where degeneracy is defined as
the presence of an infinite number of error events that all lead to the same MSED, arising from an
infinite set of possible input-sequence differences. Degenerate NSMs require special attention, as this
phenomenon can prevent guaranteed convergence of the truncated full TF, whereas the RTF effectively
mitigates this issue and remains a reliable tool for performance evaluation.
These TF analyses are also applied to optimize multi-dimensional NSMs. By extracting appropriate
1D components embedded within the higher-dimensional structures—along horizontal, vertical, and
diagonal axes in 2D grids, or Face-to-Face (F2F) (horizontal, vertical, and depth) and E2E axes in
3D grids—the MSEDs of these components can be evaluated. Maximizing the minimum among these
extracted 1D NSMs provides guidance for designing the multi-dimensional NSM filters. It should be
noted, however, that this does not strictly guarantee the overall MSED of the higher-dimensional NSM,
as error events may exist outside the extracted components. Nevertheless, this approach enables a
systematic and computationally manageable method for characterizing and optimizing NSMs, linking
simulation results, analytical bounds, and filter design in a coherent framework.
Beyond the conception and evaluation of the proposed NSMs, several structural and theoretical
aspects are worth highlighting, which reflect both the philosophy behind NSM design and their broader
implications for communication systems:
• Classical ASK and QAM modulations, whether Gray- or non-Gray-coded, are in fact particular
instances of NSMs. This underscores that the NSM framework generalizes conventional modulation
schemes while providing additional degrees of freedom for optimization.
• All NSMs presented are primarily designed for the Gaussian channel. Nevertheless, the framework
allows for potential redesigns to exploit diversity in selective or fading channels, illustrating the
adaptability of the NSM architecture to different propagation environments.
• Due to filtering, the Power Spectral Density (PSD) of NSMs is generally non-white. Scrambling
techniques can be applied to whiten the spectrum without impairing the performance metrics,
such as the MSED, thus preserving the essential characteristics of the modulation.
• Performance enhancement through increased filter lengths inevitably leads to more significant
overlap between filtered symbol contributions, which increases the Peak-to-Average Power Ratio
(PAPR) in SC systems. To mitigate this, real-valued filters may be replaced with complex-valued
6


## Page 33


filters, providing extra degrees of freedom for reducing PAPR while maintaining the desired
performance and keeping memory and complexity requirements manageable.
• The structural similarity between MS-PRSs and convolutional codes is striking. While convolutional
codes operate over discrete alphabets, typically Galois fields, NSMs operate over real or rational
sets, which motivates the designation analog convolutional codes. Classical convolutional codes
may thus be viewed as digital counterparts to MS-PRSs.
• Techniques inspired by convolutional codes, such as tail-biting, can be applied to 1D NSMs
to increase spectral efficiency without significant performance loss, by effectively reusing the
NSM structure across multiple symbol blocks. This principle naturally extends to 2D and higher-
dimensional NSMs, where the cyclic reuse of the NSM structure can be applied across the entire
2D or 3D grid, allowing the same efficiency benefits in multi-dimensional signal arrangements.
• A deep structural duality exists between NSMs and source coding using overcomplete frames and
sigma-delta quantization. Source coding transforms analog signals into bipolar symbols, while
NSMs map these bipolar symbols back to analog modulated signals. Error correction coding, such
as LDPC, operates on the bipolar symbols and naturally links source coding and NSMs. This
duality enables a unified framework where source coding, channel coding, and NSMs are efficiently
integrated, leveraging the analog and digital domains in a complementary manner for end-to-end
system design.
• Analog packing provided by NSMs and digital packing offered by error correction codes are
complementary. What analog packing can achieve efficiently in terms of packing density would
require extremely high complexity if implemented solely with digital codes, while what digital
packing can accomplish naturally and with low complexity may be very difficult or even prohibitive
for analog packing alone. By assigning tasks according to the strengths of each domain—using
analog packing where it is more efficient and digital packing where it is more natural—both
approaches support each other, leveraging the best of each. This synergy demonstrates that relying
solely on digital packing, as in conventional modulations such as 16-QAM or 64-QAM, may lead
to suboptimal performance and unnecessary complexity.
• By summing the contributions of overlapping filtered sub-streams, NSMs naturally generate
modulated symbols whose distributions increasingly resemble Gaussian distributions as filter
lengths grow. According to information theory, achieving the capacity of the Gaussian channel
requires that the channel input itself follow a Gaussian probability distribution. The NSM
framework aligns asymptotically with this fundamental optimality condition on the channel
inputs, demonstrating that as filter lengths increase, the transmitted symbols approach the
Gaussian distribution needed for capacity-approaching transmission.
• Higher-dimensional generalizations of NSMs can be constructed using analog Low-Density Gen-
erating Matrixs (LDGMs), which structurally mirror LDPC codes. This correspondence allows
NSMs to retain flexibility in filter design while benefiting from the structured sparsity of LDGM
architectures. The resulting systems facilitate a natural joint design of source coding, NSMs, and
error correction coding, producing a structured and efficient synergy between the analog and
digital domains.
Taken together, these aspects demonstrate that NSMs form a versatile and high-performance family
of modulation schemes, capable of flexible implementation across 1D and multi-dimensional systems.
7


## Page 34


By reinterpreting Mazo’s modulation and combining it with multi-stream polyphase structures and
freely chosen FIR filters, the NSM framework not only achieves strong performance but also provides
a unifying structure that bridges modulation, coding, and source representation in a coherent and
theoretically grounded manner. This extended framework naturally supports joint source coding, channel
coding, and modulation designs, highlighting the broad applicability and foundational significance of
the proposed NSMs.
Building on the framework developed above, the principal contributions of this report are summarized
below. They cover the design of new NSMs and multi-stream partial-response schemes, theoretical
and algebraic analyses (including closed-form filter characterizations and transfer-function methods),
practical optimization procedures for one- and multi-dimensional systems, and a unified architecture
that tightly integrates source coding, channel coding and modulation via analog LDGM and LDPC
structures. The main contributions are as follows:
• A variety of novel modulation schemes inspired by FTN signaling, establishing an innovative,
reunifying paradigm that enables flexible design of simple yet highly efficient modulations.
• Proposal of new MS-PRS schemes, in which a main data stream is demultiplexed and processed
through multiple parallel partial response filters. Unlike classical FTN systems, the shaping filter
used to generate the analog modulated signal can be chosen freely and independently of the
modulation scheme. Parallel filtering operations can also be freely optimized, with full control over
impulse response lengths, providing a direct handle on processing complexity and performance.
• Introduction of NSMs that are not limited to 1D or 2D structures. NSMs can naturally extend
to higher dimensions, providing additional design flexibility and favorable spatial characteristics
unavailable at lower dimensions. Some NSMs exploit fully 3D frameworks, while others combine
one-, two-, and four-dimensional architectures. In terms of performance and spectral efficiency, these
NSMs can guarantee the asymptotic performance of 2-ASK (equivalently BPSK, or equivalently
QPSK in two dimensions), while offering much higher spectral efficiencies, equivalent to those
of 4-ASK (equivalently 16-QAM in two dimensions) and 8-ASK (equivalently 64-QAM in two
dimensions).
• Design and analysis of 1D rate-2 NSMs (equivalent in spectral efficiency to 4-ASK or 16-QAM)
with real filter taps. Filters are optimized using two criteria: unconstrained average symbol energy
allocation (allowing maximum MSED) and balanced energy allocation (equal filter energies).
Unconstrained designs improve performance at the start of iterative detection (turbo-equalization),
while balanced designs enhance performance at later iterations.
• Derivation of closed-form expressions for the optimal filters and the corresponding MSEDs in
1D rate-2 NSMs with real taps. The process involves three stages: (i) numerical optimization to
approximate the best filter taps, (ii) exact determination of error events corresponding to the
MSED, and (iii) symbolic calculus exploiting the fact that these error events lead to the same
MSED, enabling closed-form determination of the filters and distances.
• Identification of minimum filter lengths required for rate-2 NSMs with real filter taps to perfectly
achieve the MSED of 2-ASK. In particular, when one of the two filters has length 1, the other
filter must have length 10 or greater in order for the scheme to reach the asymptotic bit error
probability performance of 2-ASK.
8


## Page 35


• Proposal and optimization of one-, two-, and three-dimensional rate-2 NSMs using rational (or
equivalently, integer) filter taps to achieve the 2-ASK MSED.
• Design of 1D rate-2 NSMs with bipolar non-null filter taps, where error events with SED lower
than that of 2-ASK cannot be entirely prevented, but their multiplicity decreases extremely
rapidly towards zero as the length of one filter increases while the other filter is fixed to length 1.
This vanishing multiplicity property enables these NSMs to asymptotically approach the bit error
probability performance of 2-ASK. They are thoroughly characterized algebraically using binary
Galois field tools, including primitive polynomials and m-sequences.
• Development of TFs analogous to convolutional codes. For NSMs with real taps, TFs are represented
using lists due to non-integer exponents of D, while NSMs with rational (or equivalently, integer)
taps are represented symbolically using two parameters: N (bipolar input difference Hamming
weight) and D (real output difference SED). These TFs enable tight BEP bounds, with N
instantiated as 1/2, reflecting the exponentially vanishing occurrence probability of error events as
(1/2)w, where w is the Hamming weight of the input sequence difference of the error event. This
suppression of higher Hamming-weight input differences is a surprising and innovative property,
reminiscent of the mechanism behind Parallel Concatenated Convolutional Codes (PCCCs),
although here the exponential suppression applies specifically to input sequence differences rather
than output differences as in turbo codes.
• Introduction of the RTF, a compact symbolic representation depending solely on D. It is obtained
from the full TF by taking the partial derivative with respect to N, multiplying the result by N,
and then instantiating N = 1/2. This construction simplifies analysis, particularly for NSMs with
large filter lengths or degenerate NSMs (having an infinite number of error events with identical
MSED).
• Use of sophisticated iterative algorithms applied specifically to truncated versions of the TF or to
the RTF to provide tight BEP bounds, validating simulated BER results. These algorithms operate
on numerical lists for real-tap NSMs and symbolically for rational-tap NSMs. For degenerate
NSMs, truncated RTFs enable exact iterative computation, providing reliable and tight upper
bounds where standard truncated TFs may fail.
• Partial and indirect optimization of multi-dimensional NSMs by optimizing embedded 1D NSMs
extracted along key axes of the 2D or 3D grid.
• Extension of the NSM framework to analog LDGM modulations, generalizing the classic filtered
NSM approach. Low-density integer-valued matrices are favored for implementation simplicity,
with the resulting modulation referred to as analog LDGM NSM.
• Proposal of a new architecture combining analog LDGM NSM modulation with LDPC error
correction coding. Analog LDGM NSMs possess Tanner-like bipartite graphs in the real domain,
structurally matching the Tanner graph of the associated LDPC code in the binary domain,
enabling natural and efficient turbo-detection (turbo-equalization) at the receiver. Standard
non-Gray-coded modulations (e.g., 4-ASK, 16-QAM, 8-ASK, 64-QAM) appear as particular cases
within this framework.
• Establishment of a duality between source coding using overcomplete frames with sigma-delta
quantization and the proposed MS-PRS modulations, which share a similar structural framework.

When MS-PRS modulations are generalized to analog LDGM NSMs, the overcomplete-frame-based
source coding can likewise be extended to a more general source coding paradigm using an analog
LDGM structure. This leads to a unified framework encompassing source coding, channel coding,
and modulation, where source coding employs an analog LDGM for quantization, modulation
uses another analog LDGM for signal generation, and LDPC coding links the operations. This
framework enhances both transmitter source coding and receiver demodulation performance
without requiring Gray mappings and is expected to provide groundbreaking efficiency and
performance improvements in future 6G communication systems.
The report is organized as follows:
• Section 2 provides background on the various proposed modulation schemes. It begins with
a comparison between FTN and Nyquist signaling modulations, demonstrating that FTN with
the “sinc” shaping filter, as first proposed by J. Mazo, is equivalent to MS-PRS operating at the
Nyquist signaling rate. The section then presents two illustrative examples of simple modulation
schemes that follow the MS-PRS paradigm, offering either increased data rate or enhanced
performance via an improved MSED.
• Section 3 focuses on rate-2 NSMs. The first part addresses 1D rate-2 NSMs with real-valued filter
taps, considering both unconstrained cases with unbalanced filter energies and constrained cases
with balanced filter energies. The second part is dedicated to one-, two-, and three-dimensional
rate-2 NSMs with rational (or equivalently, integer) filter taps.
• Section 4 is dedicated to rate-3 NSMs. The first part examines 1D rate-3 NSMs with real-valued
filter taps, comparing NSMs optimized independently with NSMs inherited from rate-2 designs.
The second part discusses how combining one-, two-, and four-dimensional filters within the same
rate-3 NSM can preserve the MSED of 2-ASK.
• Sections 5, 6, and 7 address NSMs with rational (or equivalently, integer) filter coefficients and
fractional rates of 3/2, 4/3, and 5/4, respectively.
• Section 8 provides a broad discussion on topics directly or indirectly related to the proposed
NSMs. Among the topics, conventional modulations—whether Gray- or non-Gray-coded—are
shown to be special cases of the NSM framework. The section also establishes an analogy between
the structure of convolutional codes and the proposed MS-PRS modulations. A key discussion
highlights the structural similarity and duality between source coding using overcomplete frames
with sigma-delta quantization and MS-PRS modulations. This similarity underpins innovative joint
designs for error correction coding and modulation, as well as unified schemes for source coding,
error correction coding, and modulation, which could significantly impact the standardization of
the 6G physical layer.

Background
2.1
Potential Ways to Increase Spectral Efficiency
In conventional communication systems, Nyquist signaling is systematically used to guarantee zero
interference between transmitted symbols. For any single- or a MC system, without guard interval
insertion, this means that the use of a frequency band of width W during a period of time T offers
10


## Page 37


2WT interference-free transmission opportunities, for real modulated symbols. As such, the only degree
of freedom left for increasing spectral efficiency is to increase the modulation order, going for example
from 2-ASK (or BPSK) to 4-ASK, for real modulated symbols, and from 4-PSK (or QPSK) to 16-QAM,
for complex modulated symbols.
For the sake presentation simplicity, we next exclusively focus on real modulated symbols. Complex
modulations of interest, such as those of famous systems like WiFi and 4G/5G, can be seen as two
parallel real modulations transmitted separately on inphase and quadrature-phase components.
When modulation order is increased in Nyquist signaling systems, in order to reach a targeted
spectral efficiency, the energy cost per transmitted bit should be significantly increased, to guarantee
the same targeted performance. Performance could be measured either theoretically, in terms of BEP
or BLock Error Probability (BLEP), or experimentally, in terms of BER or BLock Error Rate (BLER).
For example, when we go from a 2-ASK, with symbol alphabet {±1}, to a 4-ASK, with symbol
alphabet {±1, ±3}, the normalized average energy per symbol goes from 1 to 5.
This 5-fold increase in average symbol energy is due to the fact that the additional amplitudes, ±3,
added to double the offered bit rate, cost as much as 9 times the basic amplitudes, ±1, in terms of
energy. It goes without saying that this dramatic increase in energy can in no way be compensated by
the two-fold increase in binary rate offered by 4-ASK, with respect to 2-ASK. Indeed, the new energy
cost per bit is now 5/2 times that of 2-ASK, leading to a degradation of 10 log10(5/2) ≈3.98 dB. This
dramatic cost increase phenomenon remains also valid when moving from any ASK modulation to the
next ASK modulation, with twice the alphabet size.
To keep the energy cost increase to a minimum, when the offered bit rate is required to be increased,
another way to proceed is to keep the modulation order as low as possible while using FTN signaling.
For SC communications, FTN signaling leads to a compression in time by a factor α, 0 < α < 1,
meaning that the effective working symbol period is decreased to αT with respect to T, the symbol
period used for Nyquist signaling. For MC communications, besides time compression, FTN signaling
brings an additional compression in frequency by a factor β, 0 < β < 1, meaning that the working
sub-carrier spacing is decreased to βF, F being the sub-carrier spacing used in Nyquist signaling. The
overall compression factor experienced by MC systems is hence equal to αβ, offering 2WT /αβ real
modulated symbol transmission opportunities, within a frequency bandwidth W and a time duration
T . As such, the spectral efficiency gets increased by a factor of 1/αβ, every thing else being equal.
The benefits of FTN signaling, in terms of increased spectral efficiency, come always at a price. First,
SC communications experience ISI, while MC communications experience both ISI and Inter-Carrier
Interference (ICI). Secondly, the generated modulated signals can be subject to a reduction in Minimum
Euclidean Distance (MED), leading systematically to an unacceptable degradation in performance.
In 1975, Mazo [1] investigated the MED of SC binary FTN signaling and proved that the ideal
“sinc” pulse preserves modulation MED, as long as the compression factor, α, remains above 0.802. This
important result means that the offered binary rate can be boosted by 25%, at no performance loss,
and that the only penalty is in the higher receiver complexity resulting from interference processing
and suppression.
In 2009, Rusek and Anderson [7] investigated MFTN systems that use Quadrature Phase Shift Keying
(QPSK) modulation and preserve the MED, with an aggregate compression factor αβ approaching 0.5.
Nevertheless, the considered low compression factors lead to strong ISI and ICI, originating from the
nearest as well as the farthest neighbors in time-frequency, and making detection a challenging problem
at the receiver, that requires the additional help of error correction coding.

The first outstanding lesson to be learned from (2) is that FTN signaling, as proposed in [1], can
also be seen, from a different angle, as a regular Nyquist signaling, with more transmission opportunities
than modulated signal samples. By way of comparison, conventional Nyquist signaling with 4-ASK,
as portrayed by (1), offers two transmission opportunities per sample, while FTN signaling with a
compression factor α = 0.8, as illustrated in (2), offers 5 transmission opportunities for every 4 samples.
Before proceeding to other lessons and insights, it is important to underline that rewriting FTN
signals as a conventional Nyquist signals was also implicitly accomplished in the past, in [2], without
any explicit mention to that in the paper. More specifically, FTN signaling has been achieved in a vector
discrete time framework, with M transmission opportunities offered over N samples, with N < M. The
so-called transfer matrix, translating every M data inputs into N consecutive samples of the modulated
signal, sampled at the Nyquist rate, is a succession of a Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT), a filtering in
the frequency domain, using a rectangular window, and an Inverse Discrete Fourier Transform (IDFT).
As such, the N modulated signal samples, corresponding to every M data inputs, can be written in the
same way as in (2), with the nuance that the polyphase filters hm[k] are replaced by their time-aliased
counterparts.

The previous interpretation of FTN signaling as a classical Nyquist signaling, when it comes to

is subtended by a vector, which stems from a representation of the underlying time-frequency shifted

The second lesson to be learned from a comparison of (1), for Nyquist signaling, and (2), for FTN
signaling, is that, while both approaches guarantee the same (or almost the same) MED as 2-ASK,
the second transmitted bipolar input sequence, b1[l], in 4-ASK, belongs to the bipolar alphabet {±2},
and, as such, costs four times the energy of first transmitted bipolar sequence, b0[l], which has {±1}
as bipolar alphabet. Unfortunately, any attempt to reduce the corresponding contribution to energy
for 4-ASK, by using {±a}, 1 ≤a < 2, as alternative bipolar alphabet for b1[l], is accompanied by an
even more accentuated reduction in the MED. Figure 5 shows different configurations of the 4-ASK
constellation, when the parameter a goes from 2 down to 1, with a step of 0.25, in addition to a generic
configuration for an arbitrary value of a, 1 ≤a ≤2, to help assess the strong decrease in MED, as a
function of a, and compare it to the less pronounced decrease in average 4-ASK symbol energy. The
first 5 sub-figures of Figure 5 clearly show the pronounced decrease in MED when a decreases from 2
to 1, which outright vanishes to 0, when the bipolar input b1[l] reaches the same energy cost as the
bipolar input b0[l], in SFTN and MFTN. The last sub-figure of Figure 5 shows that the MED of 4-ASK,
with a, 1 ≤a ≤2 is equal to 2(a −1). Given that the average energy per 4-ASK symbol is now equal
to 1 + a2, this leads to 4(a −1)2/(1 + a2) as normalized SED. This ratio is the right measure 4-ASK
modulation at high signal-to-noise ratios. It decreases from 4/5, for conventional 4-ASK, with a = 2, to
0, for a = 1, value that precisely leads to the same cost in energy of bipolar input b1[l] as other bipolar
inputs in SFTN and MFTN.
An important question arises now. What really makes the MED stay at the level of 2-ASK, when
the 5 bipolar inputs of FTN signaling, in (2), have the same minimum energy cost, but vanishes to 0
when the 2 bipolar inputs of Nyquist signaling, in (1) are similarly set to the same minimum energy
cost? And the response, which will be corroborated in the next subsection, is particularly shocking. A
quick comparison of the forms of the filters, originating from Nyquist and FTN signaling, suggests that
the interference exhibited in FTN signaling by the IIR polyphase filters, other than h0[k], is the true
mechanism that prevents the MED from collapsing to zero, although all bipolar inputs are of common
minimum energy. This observation, which promotes interference as a technique to preserve distance, is
in complete contradiction with the common sens and the quasi unanimous attitude reported towards
interference, in most if not all past research on FTN signaling. Actually, researchers on FTN signaling
see interference as a bitter bill that must be payed in return for any increase in throughput through FTN
signaling. Additionally, they recognize the difficulty of suppressing the interference resulting from IIR
filters, such as those in (2), with a reasonable complexity and without sacrificing detection performance.
Indeed, when a “sinc” or Root Raised Cosine (RRC) filter is used, these polyphase IIR filters generally
demonstrate a slow decay in time, towards ±∞. As a consequence, their truncation in time hardly
achieves a good and satisfactory compromise between complexity and performance.
15


## Page 42


Figure 5: Constellations of 4-ASK for values of a going from 2 down to 1: (a) a = 2, (b) a = 1.75, (c)
a = 1.5, (d) a = 1.25, (e) a = 1, (f) 1 ≤a ≤2.
Another no less important question arises from the above. Is FTN signaling the best way to create
interference from performance and complexity perspectives? And the response is no. On the one hand,
for SC systems, the discrete time filter h[k] of FTN signaling (or its equivalent Nyquist signaling
polyphase filters, hm[k]) is uniquely and indirectly determined by the compression factor α, once the
transmission filter, h(t) has been chosen. This limits the number of degrees of freedom in choosing
h[k], leading typically to a discrete-time IIR filter, the truncation of which fails to achieve a good
compromise between performance and complexity. On the other hand, for MC systems, while we have
the same kind of concerns as SC systems, the resulting FTN signaling filter, h[k, l], includes a frequency
dimension, played by the parameter l, in addition to the time dimension , played by the parameter k.
This two-dimensional filter, which accounts for ICI, in addition to ISI, prevents from using any simple
trellis-based detection scheme for interference processing and suppression.
Now, using the Nyquist signaling representation framework, exemplified in (2), can we, with
maximum freedom, directly and arbitrarily choose polyphase filters to implement FTN-like systems?
Additionally, can we optimize these filters, for a targeted complexity, determined by the polyphase
filters lengths? And the common response is yes. A foretaste of this response will be made clear in the
following sub-sections.
The contradictory interpretation of the interference underlying FTN signaling, raised above, is
not the first case of its kind in the field of wireless communications. Before the advent of MIMO
wireless communications [14], the multi-path Rayleigh fading channel was considered as an unwanted
and wicked channel, as compared to the most desirable and most pleasant Gaussian channel. As
a consequence, a plethora of research work was carried on new modulation and error correction
coding schemes capable of enhancing the performance of wireless communications over Rayleigh fading
channels [15, 16, 17, 18]. This displeasing multi-path Rayleigh fading has become the cornerstone of
spatial multiplexing [19, 20, 21], one of the categories of MIMO wireless communications, which is
now an essential element of modern wireless communication standards. Spatial multiplexing is a very
16


## Page 43


powerful technique for increasing channel capacity at higher signal-to-noise ratios, that performs well
only for MIMO systems with Rayleigh fading channels.
Before moving to the experimental analysis, which will support interference as the mechanism at
the origin of enhanced modulation performance, it is very instructive, next, to make some thoughts
on FTN signaling, in relation to Nyquist signaling. Firstly, we notice that the polyphase filters, hm[k],
appearing in (2), offer, for the same truncation precision, a rough reduction by α of the number of taps
used by the unique FTN discrete filter h[k] = h(kαT). Secondly, Nyquist signaling, offers a reduction
by α of the the processing rate, compared to FTN signaling, since the former is operated at the Nyquist
rate, 1/T, while the latter is operated at rate 1/αT. Combining the two previous observations, we
can conclude that the Nyquist signaling interpretation, of any FTN signaling modulation, can offer a
substantial reduction in computational complexity.
2.3
Uncovering the Benefits of Interference through Experimentation
In what follows, we confirm, through experimental results, the importance of interference as a mechanism
to protect data inputs, when transmitting, at the same spectral efficiency as FTN signaling, using
Nyquist signaling. For simplicity sake, we focus on alternative NSMs with the same spectral efficiency
and normalized bipolar data inputs as 4-ASK. We keep the same symbolic expression for modulated
symbols, as for 4-ASK in (1), with the exception that the two filters at stake, hm[k], m = 0, 1, have
now a common length, L ≥1, and can be written as hm[k] = PL−1

A first lesson to learn from Figures 6(a)–6(d) is that artificially created interference on top of input
data sequences can, for some draws, provide some positive gain in MED, with respect to conventional
4-ASK. A second lesson is that the maximum achievable gain increases with the common filters length,
L = L0 = L1, when L goes from 2 to 5. Hence, as expected intuitively, any increase in filters length
provides additional protection to the input data sequences. A third lesson is that the optimum value,
ηo, of η, corresponding to the maximum achievable gain, should steer towards the medium value, 5/2, of
η, corresponding to input data sequences, bm[k], m = 0, 1, with the same allocated energy (η = 5 −η).
This medium value of η, if reached by ηo (this is indeed the case, as will be shown in Section 3.1),
through an increase of L, provides the same performance as 2-ASK, from a MED point of view. A
fourth lesson to draw is that this ultimate value, 5/2, of η, while being the most promising one, is
equally the most critical for some random draws of the filters, with gains going towards −∞. However,
as expected, and showcased by a comparison of Figures 6(a)-6(d), the criticality of this promising value
of η is alleviated by increasing filters length, emphasizing again the effectiveness of interference as
a mechanism for protecting input data. Another lesson to take is that conventional 4-ASK remains

To complete and close the previous discussion, it should be noted that the critical value, 5/2, of
η, which was deemed to be catastrophic for PD-NOMA, raises no concern for Code-Domain NOMA
(CD-NOMA), such as Multiuser Shared Access (MUSA) [23], Sparse Code Multiple Access (SCMA) [24],
and Low-Density Spreading (LDS) [25]. This can be explained by the fact that the codes used in
CD-NOMA introduce interference between users signals and, as such, play similar roles to the filters
used in NSMs.
Now that experimental results clearly showcase the effectiveness of interference as a mechanism for
protecting input data, we propose in the next subsection two simple, yet efficient, modulation schemes,
banking on the concept of interference protection.
2.4
Two Simple yet Efficient NSMs Advocating Interference
Our perception of interference as the right enabler for efficient modulation schemes operating at the
Nyquist signaling rate will next be supported by two simple modulation schemes. The first modulation
scheme, to be described next, will provide a foretaste of a large family of NSMs with guaranteed MED,
equal to that of 2-ASK. The second modulation scheme will provide a taster for another family of
guaranteed spectral efficiency. On the one hand, the first family of modulation schemes will, in the
sequel, be dubbed interchangeably as “minimum distance guaranteeing modulations” or “asymptotic
spectral efficiency achieving modulations.” On the other hand, the second family will be referred to as
“spectral efficiency guaranteeing modulations” or “asymptotic minimum distance achieving modulations.”
As will be made clear in Section 3.1, the intersection of these families is not empty, meaning that there
will be some NSM schemes that are simultaneously minimum-distance and spectral efficiency achieving.
2.4.1
Minimum Euclidean Distance Guaranteeing Modulation of Rate 5/4
The NSM proposed next, of rate 5/4, offers 5 transmission opportunities of bipolar input data, for every
4 symbol periods. As such, it offers the same spectral efficiency as the FTN signaling modulation with
compression factor α = 4/5 = 0.8. This value of the compression factor has the merit of being both
rational and near the Mazo limit, 0.802, guaranteeing no loss in MED with respect to 2-ASK.

To alleviate the notations, we omit, in what follows, the indexing parameter l in the expressions of
s[l] and b[l]. Next, we prove that the MED of 2-ASK is preserved by the proposed NSM scheme. For
that, we need to show that the squared Euclidean norm of the modulated block difference, ∆s ≜s1 −s0,
corresponding to the non-null input block difference, ∆b ≜b1 −b0, of two different input blocks, b0
and b1, is always greater than or equal to 4.
Firstly, we consider the case where the last component of ∆b is null. This case corresponds exactly
to that of 2-ASK, and at least one component of ∆s is in {±2}, because at least one of the 4 first
components, ∆b is non-null, and therefore equal to ±2. Hence, the squared Euclidean norm of ∆s is at
least equal to 4.
Secondly, we consider the case where the last component of ∆b is non-null, and therefore equal
to ±2. In this case, since the entries corresponding to the last raw of the generating matrix G are
all equal to 1/2, the contributions of the first 4 components of ∆b to ∆s, which are in {0, ±2}, are
shifted by either +1 or −1. Therefore, the modulated block difference, ∆s, has its components in the
set {±1, ±3}. It follows that all components of ∆s have a modulus greater than or equal to 1. Since ∆s
has 4 such components, it follows that the squared Euclidean norm of ∆s is also at least equal to 4 in
this case. This establishes the fact that the proposed modulation scheme preserves the MED of 4-ASK.
The previous considerations, which led to the determination of the MSED of the modulation at
hand, remain unchanged, if any of the non-null entries of generating matrix G changes sign. Hence, we
can freely change the sign of any of the non-null entries of G, without altering the modulation MED.
As depicted in Figure 8, we, next, assess the performance of the proposed NSM, through an
evaluation of the achieved BER. For comparison purpose, we also evaluate the BER of the Mazo “sinc”
based FTN signaling, with a compression factor, α, of 0.8 and filter truncation lengths, LM and LD,
at the modulator and the demodulator, respectively. On the one hand, the modulator’s truncated
filter length, LM, must be large enough to meet power spectrum mask requirements, while remaining
small enough to maintain reasonable filtering complexity at the transmitter. On the other hand, the
demodulator’s truncated filter length, LD, must be large enough to capture most of the useful energy
conveyed by each transmitted symbol and, as a result, reduce residual ISI, while remaining small enough
to maintain affordable equalization complexity at the receiver.
Notice that the modulator’s filtering complexity is always proportional to the corresponding
truncated filter length LM. Also take note that the demodulation complexity can be kept proportional

2.4.2
Spectral Efficiency Guaranteeing Modulation of Rate 2
Before moving on to the description and characterization of the illustrative NSM of rate 2, it is considered
to be highly helpful to have a brief discussion on some relevant aspects of NSMs.
In the first place, it is important to keep in mind that any NSM only requires the specification of
the filters, up to an arbitrary non-null multiplicative factor. So, if, for a particular multiplicative factor,
23


## Page 50


ε, the scaled filters, ˚hm[k] = ε¯hm[k], have simpler expressions than the normalized filters, ¯hm[k], then
they can be extremely insightful when designing and characterizing NSMs.
Second, for an infinite train of input bipolar data, Nyquist signaling systems with different filters can
be perfectly equivalent in terms of characteristics and performance. The opposite, −hm[k], of any of the
filters, hm[k], preserves Nyquist signaling system characteristics and performance. Furthermore, shifting
in time any of the filters by an arbitrary time advance or time delay has no effect on performance.
Besides, time reversal, in which all filters, hm[k] = PL−1
l=0 hm[l]δ[k −l], are replaced by their time
reversal counterparts, h−

characteristics and performance. Also, alternately changing the signs of the coefficients of an arbitrary
filter, hm[l], yields the equivalent filter ˜hm[l] = PL−1
l=0 (−1)lhm[l]δ[k −l]. To see this, consider the fact
that if an input sequence difference, ∆b[k], leads to the modulated sequence difference ∆s[k], when
filtered by hm[l], then the alternate input sequence difference, ∆˜b[k] ≜(−1)k∆b[k], leads to the alternate
modulated sequence difference, ∆˜s[k] = (−1)k∆s[k], which has precisely the same norm. To finish, it is
crucial to remember that the equivalence ceases for several of the previous filter operations, when input
data sequences of finite lengths are taken into account.
In light of the foregoing, we will now explore the intuitive derivation of one of the most straightforward
rate-2 NSMs. This derivation can be made by just modifying one of the filters, hm[k] = 2mδ[k], m = 0, 1,
that are used in traditional 4-ASK. For this, notice the important discrepancy in conveyed modulated
signal energy between h1[k] and h0[k], with the former bearing four times as much energy as the latter.
The proposed Nyquist signaling rate-2 modulation addresses this disparity in conveyed energy by
keeping the most energetic filter, h1[k], as it is and replacing the least energetic filter, h0[k] = δ[k], with
a two-fold more energetic filter. More specifically, in their simplest scaled forms, the proposed filters are
˚h0[k] = δ[k] + δ[k −1] and ˚h1[k] = 2δ[k], resulting in a reduction by a factor of two of the discrepancy.
