The first type of error events of maximum multiplicity contributions are those where ∆˚b0[k] = 0
and ∆˚b1[k] = ±δ[k]. It corresponds to output difference sequences ∆¯s[k] = ±2δ[k]. Its contribution to
the transfer function, with regards to the second MSED, is given by 2N.
The second type of error events of maximum multiplicity contributions are those where ∆˚b0[k] =
αδ[k], with α ∈{±1}. In this case, there are 16 authorized input difference sequences, ∆˚b1[k], that

˚h0[k] = h0[0]δ[k] + h0[k1]δ[k −k1] + h0[k2]δ[k −k2] + h0[L0 −1]δ[k −(L0 −1)], where 0 < k1 <
k2 < L0 −1. Then, the 16 allowed input difference sequences, ∆˚b1[k], are of the form ∆˚b1[k] =
∆˚b1[0]δ[k]+∆˚b1[k1]δ[k−k1]+∆˚b1[k2]δ[k−k2]+∆˚b1[L0−1]δ[k−(L0−1)], where ∆˚b1[k] ∈{0, −αh0[k]},

number stems from the tightness property inherited from the peculiar choice of the filters coefficients.
Their contribution to the transfer function, with regards to the second MSED, is given by 2N(1 + N)4.

regards to the second MSED, is equal to

the relatively huge multiplicity of 205
32 , obtained in (190). Remember that this huge multiplicity arises
from the tightness property underlying filters ˚h0[k] = δ[k] ± δ[k −k0] ± δ[k −k1] ± δ[k −L0 + 1] and
˚h1[k] = 2δ[k]. As a consequence, to reduce it, the best way is to chose filters that do not show tightness.
Keeping in mind that filters ˚h0[k] and ˚h1[k] must present the same energy (same SEN) and integer
coefficients, immediate efficient choices can be obtained by taking ˚h1[k] = 3δ[k] or 5δ[k].
To avoid tightness conditions for the former choice, where ˚h1[k] = 3δ[k], the coefficients of filter
˚h0[k] should be exclusively in the set {0, ±1}. Being of the same SEN as ˚h1[k], which is equal to 9, this
filter must show 9 non-null coefficients in the set {±1}. As a consequence, L0 mus be at least equal to
9. NSMs with these filters are expected to present strictly lower MSEDs than 2-ASK. However, the

cumulative of the multiplicities of all error events, with lower SED than 2-ASK, can be made very small

of these error events, through an adequate choice of filter ˚h0[k]. This aspect can be studied in detail
by casting all involved differences sequences into equivalent ones in the Galois field GF(3) = {0, 1, 2},
using modular 3 arithmetic.
For the latter choice, where ˚h1[k] = 5δ[k], the coefficients of filter ˚h0[k] should be exclusively in the
set {0, ±1, ±2}. The equality constraint for the squared Euclidean norms of ˚h0[k] and ˚h1[k] requires
that ˚h0[k] has 25 as SEN. On the one hand, the candidate filters ˚h0[k], with the smallest number
of non-null coefficients, should have exactly 6 non-null coefficients in the set {±2} and one non-null
coefficient in the set {±1}. The corresponding minimum filter length is therefore lower bounded by
7. On the other hand, the candidate filters ˚h0[k], with the largest number of non-null coefficients,
should have 25 non-null coefficients in the set {±1}. Obviously, the minimum filter length for ˚h0[k] is
L0 = 25. Intermediate candidate filters can be obtained by replacing any non-null coefficient in ˚h0[k],
in the set {±2} by four non-null coefficients in the set {±1}. The discussions above, for the case where
˚h1[k] = 3δ[k], apply here. We can use modular arithmetic in the Galois field GF(5) = {0, 1, 2, 3, 4}.

Tight Estimate of the BEP for the Rate-3/2 NSM
The procedure for deriving a close estimate of the BEP for the rate-3/2 NSM is identical to that in
Appendix B, for the rate-2 NSM described in Subsection 2.4.2. To begin, we determine the NSM TF,
T(N, D), using the state diagram of the input/output sequence differences given in Figure 81(a), arising
from the trellis section shown in Figure 55(b). Similar to the trellis section in Figure 55(b), each branch
in this state diagram has an input/output label of the form ∆¯b0[k] ∆¯b1[k] ∆¯b2[k]/∆˚s[2k] ∆˚s[2k + 1].
Because we want to identify every error event that could lead to demodulator decision errors, we’ve
shown the “null” branch, with labels 000/00, as a dashed line in Figure 81(a). This branch, which is
also shown as a dashed line in Figures 81(b)–81(d), should not be a part of any error event and, as a
result, should not be taken into account when calculating the TF.
In order to move forward with the derivation of the rate-3/2 NSM TF, we rename, in Figure 81(b),
the branches of the state diagram of Figure 81(a), by assigning labels of the form NiDj. In each branch
in the state diagram of Figure 81(b), with label NiDj, i represents the number of non-null components
in ∆¯b0[k] ∆¯b1[k] ∆¯b2[k], while j represents the squared norm of (∆˚s[2k], ∆˚s[2k + 1]).
To simplify the calculation of the TF, T(N, D), we begin by aggregating, in Figure 81(c), the labels
of the branches in Figure 81(b) which begin in a common state and end in a common state. Evidently,
the “null” branch, labeled N0D0 = 1, which should be ignored for the TF expression, is not merged
with the other branches departing from and arriving at the same 0 state.
To further simplify the derivation of the said TF, states −2 and +2, which play identical roles in
terms of aggregate branch labels, are merged, in Figure 81(d), into a single state, named ±2. Because
of this, in Figure 81(c), the labels of branches connecting state 0 to states −2 and +2 are aggregated,
and labels of branches leaving state −2 to state +2 or state +2 to state −2 are replaced by a single
branch with the same label that starts and ends at the same aggregate state, ±2.
The final step before finding the TF, as illustrated in Figure 81(e), is to remove the “null” branch,
labeled 1, and split the 0 state into a starting state, labeled 0s, and an ending state, labeled 0e.

The suggested rate-3/2 NSM’s tight estimate of the BEP, provided in (58), is obtained by preserving
only error events with minimum squared Euclidean distance. With 2-ASK as a reference, the multiplicity
factor, 65, in (194), must be divided by three because three bipolar symbols are sent at each section of the
NSM’s trellis, shown in Figure 54(b). However, unlike the rate-2 NSM discussed in Subsection 2.4.2, it
does not require any normalization within the square-root argument of the error function complementary,
erfc(·), because all three bipolar symbols use filters with identical energies and are thus transmitted
with the same average energy.
To conclude this appendix, it is important to note that the multiplicity of the BEP of the rate-3/2
modulation, in (12), has increased explosively to 65/3 as contrasted to the multiplicity of 1, for 2-ASK.
This expected result is due to two different sorts of degeneration, which are more clearly visible when
looking at the transitions in the input/output sequence trellis in Figure 55(b). On the one hand, with a
non-null input difference of −2 + 2 + 2 (respectively, +2 −2 −2), but a null output difference of 00, the
branch connecting state −2 (respectively, +2) to itself is the cause of the first type of degeneration.
Due to the fact that all three input differences are simultaneously non-null, in the set {±2}, transiting
over such a branches happens with a relatively low probability of ( 1
2)3. On the other hand, with a
non-null input difference of +200 (respectively, −200), but a null output difference of 00, the branch
connecting state −2 (respectively, +2) to state +2 (respectively, −2) is the cause of the second type of
degeneration. This kind of degeneration is closely related to the quincunx alternating-sign error event
that has been pointed out in Subsection 3.2.2. Because it happens with a larger probability of 1/2, its
contribution to the multiplicity factor in the approximate expression of the BEP is greater than that of
the first type of degeneration.

Symbolic Determination of the RTFs of Rate-(Q+1)/Q NSMs
The iterative determination of the truncated TF, T(N, D; P), of rate-2 NSMs, described in Subsection D.2
of Appendix D, and achieved in Algorithm 7, was affordable numerically. The requirement to have
L1 > 1, in addition to L0 > 1, was indeed a perfect configuration since it prevented parallel branches
between any two states in the state diagram.
When L1 = 1, which is a pretty common arrangement in this study, parallel branches between any
two connected states in the state diagram, cannot be avoided anymore. For any rate-(Q + 1)/Q NSM,
Q ≥1, state diagram admits two possible configurations. In the first configuration, any two connected
states, σ′ and σ, are bound by 3Q parallel branches, corresponding to the 3Q possible values taken
by Q consecutive input sequence difference, ∆¯b1[k], with components in the ternary set {0, ±2}. An
example of such a state diagram configuration is shown in Figures 81(a) and 81(b), for the rate-3/2
NSM with Q = 2 and 3Q = 9 parallel branches between any two connected states, studied in Section 5.
This first state diagram configuration is adopted in Algorithm 10 for the symbolic determination of the
RTF, ˙T(D), of an arbitrary rate-(Q + 1)/Q NSM.

For the symbolic determination of the RTF, ˙T(D), of any rate-(Q + 1)/Q NSM, we rely on a
modified state diagram, similar to the one introduced in Appendix D. This modified state diagram is
obtained by removing the unique branch looping into the zero state, 0, and splitting this zero state into
a starting zero state, 0s, and an ending state, 0e. Due to the two roles that the zero state, 0, plays in the
modified state diagram, we introduce the two new sets of states, Σs ≜Σ∗∪{0s} and Σe ≜Σ∗∪{0e},
where, as in Appendices C and D, Σ∗denotes the set of all intermediate states, excluding the split zero
states 0s and 0e. For completeness, we also need the set of all sets, Σ = Σ∗∪{0}, in the original state
diagram. Notice that Σs, Σe and Σ have a common size |Σs| = |Σe| = |Σ| = 3M−1, where M ≜L0/Q.

where 0|Σ|×|Σ| is the |Σ| × |Σ| null matrix. After solving (196), the desired RTF, ˙T(D), is determined
as ˙T(D) = ˙T0e(D), ˙T0e(D) being the component of T e, associated to ending state, 0e.
As demonstrated in Algorithm 10, this linear system of 2|Σ| unknowns implies the processing of
a 2|Σ| × 2|Σ| square matrix. The size of this matrix explodes exponentially as M = L0/Q increases,
leading to an explosion of symbolic computation complexity, when L0 increases, for a given value of Q,
and therefore a given NSM rate ρ = (Q + 1)/Q.
One way to simplify the resolution, of symbolic matrix system (196), is to proceed in two steps,
by solving for T e(D) first, using equation T e(D) = T s(D)L(D), and ˙T e(D) second, using equation
˙T e(D) = T s(D) ˙L(D) + ˙T s(D)L(D). This two-step approach reduces the common size of involved
matrices by half, with respect to the original approach, leading to a significant reduction in complexity,
even though it requires the processing to be repeated twice.
Another different way to reduce the complexity of the symbolic derivation of the RTF, is to
notice that Lσ′σ(D) = L−σ′,−σ(D) for any pair of states, (σ′, σ) in ¯Σ ≜Σ∗∪{0s, 0e}. Based on this
observation, we can affirm that the solutions, Tσ(D) and ˙Tσ(D), σ ∈Σ∗, to the symbolic equations
in (195) and symbolic matrix equation in (196), is such that Tσ(D) = T−σ(D) and ˙Tσ(D) = ˙T−σ(D),
σ ∈¯Σ. In light of this, the set of states Σ∗must be split into two complementary subsets, Σ+∗and
Σ−∗= −Σ+∗≜{−σ | σ ∈Σ+∗}, such that Σ+∗∪Σ−∗= Σ∗and Σ+∗∩Σ−∗= ∅. Without loss of
generality, we can define Σ+∗as the set of non-null states with positive first non-null component. In
this case, Σ−∗will be the set of non-null states with negative first non-null component. Clearly, subsets
Σ+∗and Σ−∗have a common size, |Σ+∗| = |Σ−∗| = |Σ∗|/2 = (3M−1 −1)/2.

Algorithm 11 has been successfully utilized to derive the truncated version, ˙T(D; P), to order P, of
the RTF, ˙T(D), of the majority of the NSMs listed in Tables 47—72. However, for some rate-(Q + 1)/Q
NSMs, this algorithm, which was implemented in Matlab, failed to yield a solution, even after a
significant length of time. We therefore turned to Algorithm 12, which has the benefit of never failing,
in such circumstances.
The Matlab implementations of Algorithms 11 and 12 have been validated by comparing the first
terms of the RTF ˙T(D), calculated experimentally, in Table 47, and theoretically, in (194), for filter
˚h0[k] = δ[k] + δ[k −1] + δ[k −2] + δ[k −3].

## Page 363


Biographies
Mohamed Siala received the engineering degree from École Polytechnique, Palaiseau,
France, in 1988, the telecommunications engineering degree from Télécom Paris, Paris,
France, in 1990, and the Ph.D. degree in digital communications from Télécom Paris
in 1995, with a focus on coding for the magnetic recording channel. From 1990 to
2001, he worked in France at Alcatel Radio-Téléphones, Wavecom, and Orange Labs
on GSM physical-layer design, channel estimation techniques for the INMARSAT ICO
mobile satellite system, and the development and standardization of 3G radio interfaces. Since 2001, he
has been with the Higher School of Communications of Tunis (SUP’COM), Tunisia, where he is currently
a Professor in the Department of Applied Mathematics, Signals, and Communications. His research
interests include multicarrier modulation, waveform design, channel estimation and synchronization,
MIMO systems, adaptive transmission, and cooperative and cognitive radio networks.
Abdullah Al-Nafisah holds an M.S. degree in Electrical and Computer Engineering
from King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST). He earned a
double major with highest honors in Electrical Engineering and Physics from King
Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals (KFUPM). His research interests include
RF electronics and signal processing for telecommunications. He has worked on chaotic
circuits with an emphasis on practical, low-cost designs for synchronous and secure
communications. Also, he developed a novel CFOA-based filter circuit with a tunable bandwidth. He is
currently working on real-time FPGA systems for different research projects.
Tareq Al-Naffouri received the B.S. (Honors) degree in Mathematics and Electrical
Engineering from King Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals (KFUPM), Saudi
Arabia. He obtained the M.S. degree in Electrical Engineering from the Georgia
Institute of Technology, USA, in 1998, and the Ph.D. degree in Electrical Engineering
from Stanford University, USA, in 2004. He has held visiting scholar appointments at
the California Institute of Technology (2005–2006) and served as a Fulbright Scholar at
the University of Southern California (2008). He is currently a Professor in the Electrical and Computer
Engineering Program at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST), Saudi Arabia,
and Principal Investigator of the Information Science Lab. His research interests include sparse, adaptive,
and statistical signal processing, with applications to wireless communications, localization, inference
and learning, smart cities, and IoT-enabled networks.
